It was found that these failures were mainly associated with a flawed tank design and fabrication of the tank floor, leading to high stress, stress relaxation cracking (SRC), buckling, low cycle fatigue (LCF), and creep [4]. Tank designers and constructors currently rely on existing standards like API 650 supplemented by ASME BPVC; however, this approach has proven to have limitations for the high temperatures, thermal cycling, and transient conditions unique to the CSP application. New standards like the ASME TES-1-2023 – ‘Safety Standard for Thermal Energy Storage Systems: Molten Salts’ [5] have been developed. This standard establishes the safety-related criteria and high-level requirements for the design and construction of molten salt systems; however, it does not provide prescriptive, step-by-step technical guidelines on how the specific construction, welding, and fabrication procedures should be executed, often deferring those execution details to established industry practice. The first project report for the DOE SETO-funded project, agreement DE-EE0038475, published in March 2024 [4], outlined a comprehensive path for future research, suggesting several alternatives regarding tank design, fabrication, operation, and commissioning. Two of these alternatives—tank size and the preheating process—were initially explored within the project, and their results are presented in this current report. Motivated by CSP industry trends toward multiple, smaller tanks (typically below 30 meters in diameter), this analysis explored the impact of tank size. This approach represents a departure from the ~41-meter diameter commercial tanks employed at plants such as Crescent Dunes and Noor III. The study specifically considered tanks with varying diameters and floor thicknesses and their effect on stress distribution in the tank floor. In addition to tank size, industry evidence suggested that the preheating process could strongly influence both residual stress relief and the susceptibility to floor buckling [6]. Therefore, the project also focused on analyzing the stress distribution and deformation of the tank floor during a typical preheating process and provides a general description of tank preheating. 1.2 Factors Affecting Tank Integrity Drawing on extensive research and experience with commercial Concentrating Solar Power (CSP) plants, the project team identified four primary failure modes in SS 347H molten salt hot tanks: Low Cycle Fatigue (LCF), Stress Relaxation Cracking (SRC), creep, and buckling, Figure 1. These failures result from a dangerous confluence of several major factors related to design, fabrication, and operation. Key design and fabrication deficiencies include a floor design prone to buckling, defects in weldments (like lack of fusion), the selection of the SRC-susceptible E347 filler material, and non-optimal welding procedures that introduce high residual stresses in the tank floor.
